title: Frequency density from a class frequency and width
source: S1 Ch1 theory S1-1.3 Quick check 1 (class width 8, frequency 24, frequency density 3)
stem: A class of width {w|int} contains {f|int} observations. Find the frequency density.

steps.name: form
steps.text_tex: Frequency density \(=\) class frequency \(\div\) class width \(=\dfrac{{f|int}}{{w|int}}\).

contexts.stem: The masses in a class of width {w|int} kg have frequency {f|int}. What is the frequency density, in observations per kilogram?
A class of times has width {w|int} minutes and contains {f|int} recorded times. Find the frequency density, in times per minute.

title: Class frequency from frequency density and width
source: S1 Ch1 theory S1-1.3 Quick check 2 (fd 3, width 10, frequency 30)
stem: A histogram column has frequency density {d|int} and class width {w|int}. How many observations does the column represent?

steps.name: form
steps.text_tex: Class frequency \(=\) class width \(\times\) frequency density \(={w|int}\times{d|int}\).

contexts.stem: On a histogram of heights, one column has frequency density {d|int} and width {w|int} cm. Find the frequency of that class.
A histogram of parcel masses has a column of width {w|int} kg and frequency density {d|int} parcels per kilogram. How many parcels are in that class?

title: Estimate a frequency from part of a class, assuming even spread
source: S1 Ch1 theory S1-1.3 Quick check 3 (class width 20, frequency 48, first 5 units, estimate 12)
stem: A class of width {w|int} contains {f|int} observations, assumed spread evenly through the class. Estimate the number of observations in a sub-interval of width {p|int} at one end of the class.

steps.name: form
steps.text_tex: The sub-interval is a fraction \(\dfrac{{p|int}}{{w|int}}\) of the class, so the estimate is \(\dfrac{{p|int}}{{w|int}}\times{f|int}\).
steps.note: Scale the class frequency by the width fraction.

title: Find a and b in a frequency-density table of delivery times

source.note: Stem verbatim from the QP PDF (the times are correct to the nearest minute). Steps and marks from the official MS PDF. Independently: class widths from the boundaries are 3, 2, 3 and 4, so a=9/2=4.5 and b=1.5*4=6. Part (ii), drawing the histogram, is omitted. Fully manual, because the official part asks for two values and the engine has one auto-marked number per part.

stem:
Robert has a part-time job delivering newspapers. On a number of days he noted the time, correct to the nearest minute, that it took him to do his job. Robert used his results to draw up the following table; two of the values in the table are denoted by \(a\) and \(b\).
Time (\(t\) minutes): \(60-62\), \(63-64\), \(65-67\), \(68-71\).
Frequency (number of days): \(3\), \(9\), \(6\), \(b\).
Frequency density: \(1\), \(a\), \(2\), \(1.5\).
Find the values of \(a\) and \(b\).

steps.name: fd
steps.text_tex: The times are to the nearest minute, so the class widths from the boundaries are \(3\), \(2\), \(3\) and \(4\). Frequency density \(=\) frequency \(\div\) class width, so \(a=9\div 2\).

steps.name: b
steps.note: MS: A1 Correct b, 1.5=b/4 so b=6.

title: Two reasons why Dominic’s diagram is not a correct histogram

source.note: Stem verbatim from the QP PDF, including the table. The official diagram is described from the rendered QP page (vertical axis labelled Number of students; bars of heights 18, 13, 8, 12 and 4 over 1–3, 4–5, 6–8, 9–11 and 12–16, with gaps). A reconstruction of that official figure is in assets/S1-1.3-pp-9709-63-ON13-Q1-dominic.svg for optional display. Steps and marks from the official MS PDF. Fully manual.

stem:
The distance of a student’s home from college, correct to the nearest kilometre, was recorded for each of 55 students. The distances are summarised in the following table.
Distance from college (km): \(1-3\), \(4-5\), \(6-8\), \(9-11\), \(12-16\).
Number of students: \(18\), \(13\), \(8\), \(12\), \(4\).
Dominic is asked to draw a histogram to illustrate the data. Dominic’s diagram has the vertical axis labelled “Number of students”. Separate bars of heights 18, 13, 8, 12 and 4 stand over the intervals 1 to 3, 4 to 5, 6 to 8, 9 to 11 and 12 to 16, with gaps between neighbouring bars.
Give two reasons why this is not a correct histogram.

steps.name: gaps
steps.text_tex: The bars are not touching. In a histogram there are no gaps between classes unless a class has frequency zero; the classes should meet at the class boundaries (for data to the nearest kilometre, at \(0.5\), \(3.5\), and so on).
steps.note: MS: B1 bars are not touching oe. Sensible reason involving not touching, no gaps, class boundaries, group data not continuous (may be the negative).

steps.name: fd
steps.text_tex: The vertical axis is labelled “Number of students”, and the bar heights are the frequencies. In a histogram the vertical axis must be frequency density, so that area represents frequency.
steps.note: MS: B1 Area not rep by frequency, not used fd, not labelled fd. Must be frequency density oe. Wrong height not sufficient. (Best 2 reasons awarded).
